subject: react
title: Components and JSX
summary: Read and compose function components, pass data through props, render lists with stable keys, and add independent interactive state.

lessons.title: Components describe the screen
lessons.summary: Read a function component and trace how nested components form a user interface.
lessons.body:
React is a JavaScript library for building a **user interface**: the things a person sees and interacts with. A **component** describes one part of that interface. It might be a heading, a task row or an entire screen. Starting with small named parts makes a larger screen easier to read and reuse. This course assumes basic JavaScript variables, functions, arrays and objects. It explains the extra syntax as it appears. Examples belong in a React-enabled project or playground whose build tool transforms JSX into JavaScript; pasting JSX directly into an ordinary browser script will not work. Project installation is outside this course. ## A function that describes UI A function component returns a description of what should appear. **JSX** is the HTML-like syntax inside the JavaScript below. HTML is the browser's document markup language; JSX is JavaScript syntax that a tool transforms. They look similar but are not interchangeable. This complete component file can be used as the root component in that prepared environment. `export default` makes `StudyPage` available for another file to import. The environment mounts that root component into the page. ```jsx function Welcome() { return

Ready to study?

; } export default function StudyPage() { return (

My study app

); } ``` `StudyPage` returns one `main` element containing a heading and two uses of `Welcome`. Each use describes an `h2` with the same text. The browser therefore displays the main heading followed by two smaller headings. Writing a function definition alone does not put it on the screen: some rendered component must use it. `` tells React to use the JavaScript component named `Welcome`. `
` and `

` refer to built-in browser elements. Names used as custom JSX tags must begin with a capital letter. Writing `` would describe a lowercase element rather than call the `Welcome` component. The parentheses after `return` group several lines into one returned expression. Keep the opening parenthesis on the same line as `return`; JavaScript can otherwise end the return statement before the markup. ## Compose a screen from parts **Composition** means combining smaller components to make a larger one. A component can contain ordinary elements and other components. Keep component definitions at the top level of a file, rather than defining one inside another component's function. This gives the component a stable definition; later lessons explain why component identity matters for state. > [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A reusable recipe > A recipe for a sandwich can be used twice when preparing two lunches. > > **How it maps:** The component function is the reusable description; each JSX use asks React for another instance of that part of the interface. > > **Where it stops:** A component returns a UI description, not a physical object. React decides when to run it and how to update the browser. Choose a component when a part has a clear responsibility or is reused. You do not need to make every single tag a separate component. A useful boundary lets you understand its purpose from its name and inputs. ## Key takeaways - A function component describes a piece of UI by returning JSX. - Capitalised JSX names refer to components; lowercase names are treated as browser element names. - Nesting and reusing components is composition. - Use a React-enabled environment that transforms JSX before the browser runs it. ## Further reading - [Your first component — React](https://react.dev/learn/your-first-component) - [Importing and exporting components — React](https://react.dev/learn/importing-and-exporting-components)

lessons.title: Write valid JSX
lessons.summary: Use fragments, closed tags, className and style objects without confusing JSX with HTML.
lessons.body:
JSX describes elements using familiar tag shapes, but a JavaScript tool must be able to read it as an expression. A few consistent rules prevent most beginner syntax errors. React and JSX are separate ideas: React is the UI library; JSX is an optional way of writing its element descriptions. ## Group and close the markup A component returning several neighbouring elements must group them into one returned value. A wrapper such as `section` works when that element belongs in the page structure. A **fragment**, written `<>...`, groups neighbouring elements without adding a wrapper element to the browser's DOM. The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the browser's live tree of DOM nodes. A fragment changes the JSX grouping without creating a new node in that tree. It is useful when a wrapper would be meaningless, but it does not supply layout or styling of its own. Every JSX tag must close. Write `
` rather than `
` and `
  • Read
    • ` rather than leaving the closing tag out. Paired tags must nest properly: close the inner element before the outer one. This is stricter than some HTML shorthand. ## Use JavaScript attribute names Use **className** for an element's CSS class. CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, controls appearance; a class name chooses styling rules defined elsewhere. Most React DOM property names use camelCase: words join with later words starting in capitals. `onClick` is an example you will meet in the events lesson. Accessibility attributes such as `aria-label`, and custom `data-*` attributes, retain their hyphens. For an inline **style**, pass a JavaScript object rather than an HTML style string. Its property names are generally camelCase, such as `backgroundColor`. The outer braces enter JavaScript from JSX; the inner braces create the object. They are two separate uses of JavaScript syntax, not a special double-brace operator. This component excerpt uses a fragment and explicit CSS string values. The `notice` class can be defined in the project's stylesheet. ```jsx function Notice() { return ( <>

    Next step

    Read the lesson.
    Then try its questions.

    ); } ``` The DOM contains a heading and a paragraph as siblings. The line break is a child of the paragraph. The fragment does not become an extra `div`. `className="notice"` sets the heading's class; it does not create a new component called `notice`. A common debugging sequence is to check the returned grouping, then matching tags, then attribute names. A syntax error prevents the file being transformed at all, so do this before investigating state or event behaviour. Valid JSX describes structure; visual layout still depends on the browser and CSS. ## Key takeaways - Group neighbouring returned elements with a meaningful wrapper or a fragment. - Close every JSX tag, including tags such as `br`. - Use `className` and camelCase style properties. - A `style` value is an object; a fragment adds no DOM wrapper. ## Further reading - [Writing markup with JSX — React](https://react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx) - [JavaScript in JSX with curly braces — React](https://react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces)

lessons.title: Props and reusable composition
lessons.summary: Pass read-only inputs and nested children into a reusable card component.
lessons.body:
A reusable component should describe the same kind of UI with different content. **Props**, short for properties, are the inputs that a parent passes to a child component. A prop can hold a string, number, boolean, object, array, function or JSX value. Props are not limited to HTML attributes. ## Read inputs without changing them A component receives one props object. Destructuring its parameter gives local names to chosen properties. Props are **read-only**: treat both the props object and values passed through it as immutable inputs. Do not assign a different title or change an array received from a parent while rendering. Read-only is a programming rule, not a claim that every JavaScript object is deeply frozen. A parent can later render the child with different props. When that happens, the child describes the UI using those new inputs. If the child needs an interaction to request a change, the parent can pass a callback; later lessons develop that pattern. ## Let the caller supply the inside **children** is the prop containing JSX nested between a component's opening and closing tags. A wrapper can place those children inside its own layout without knowing their detailed content. This is composition: the caller decides the content and the wrapper decides the surrounding structure. This complete component file renders two cards. `title = 'Untitled'` is a JavaScript default parameter inside destructuring. That default is used when the prop is missing or `undefined`, but not when it is `null` or an empty string. ```jsx function Card({ title = 'Untitled', children }) { return (

{title}

{children}
); } export default function App() { return (

Read one lesson.
); } ``` The first card shows `Today` and a paragraph. The second shows `Untitled` and a button. `Card` does not need separate branches for paragraphs and buttons: it simply includes its `children` where the content belongs. The button is presentational here; a later lesson gives it an event handler. The parent uses an explicit title prop and nested JSX for different jobs. `title` supplies one named value; `children` supplies the flexible content region. Neither changes who owns the data: the parent chooses what it passes, while the child reads it. > [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A picture frame > One frame design can surround different pictures and carry different captions. > > **How it maps:** The wrapper component supplies the frame, a named prop supplies the caption and `children` supplies the picture placed inside. > > **Where it stops:** Children are React values describing content, not objects physically inserted into a frame. The parent can provide new values on another render. Prefer clear named props over passing a large object that the component does not need. If a card only needs a title, receiving that title directly makes its contract easier to see. Composition helps avoid a single component accumulating a different boolean prop for every possible layout. ## Key takeaways - Props flow from parent to child as read-only inputs. - Nested JSX arrives through the `children` prop. - Defaults apply to missing or `undefined` props, not `null`. - Compose a reusable wrapper with caller-supplied content. ## Further reading - [Passing props to a component — React](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component)

lessons.title: Lists and stable keys
lessons.summary: Transform arrays into elements and choose keys that keep each item associated with its identity.
lessons.body:
A task list should come from task data rather than repeated handwritten tags. JavaScript array methods choose which records to show and transform them into JSX. React also needs a reliable way to match items between renders when a list changes. ## Filter records, then map them Array **filter** returns a new array containing items whose callback returned a truthy value. Array **map** returns a new array containing each callback's result. Neither method inherently changes the source array, although a callback can still incorrectly mutate the objects it receives. This component excerpt receives a `tasks` array. Each record has a stable string `id`, a `title` and a boolean `done`. The arrow callback with parentheses implicitly returns its JSX. ```jsx function OpenTasks({ tasks }) { const open = tasks.filter( task => !task.done ); return (
    {open.map(task => (
  • {task.title}
    • ))}
); } ``` Suppose the records are `a: Read` (open), `b: Rest` (done) and `c: Practise` (open). Filtering keeps records `a` and `c`. Mapping returns two list elements, displaying `Read` and `Practise`. The original array still contains all three records. ## Give each sibling a stable identity A **React key** is an identity hint for an element in a collection of siblings. It helps React match a record's previous UI to its next UI when items are inserted, removed or reordered. Put the key on the element returned directly from `map`; a key buried inside a child component is too far down. Keys must be unique among siblings and stable for the same item across renders. They need not be globally unique across separate lists. Use an identifier from the data. Create an identifier when creating a new record, rather than generating a random key during rendering. Random keys change on each render and can cause React to recreate items, losing user input or component state. The array **index** is an item's current position, not its identity. Imagine rows A and B each have a text input. Someone edits A's input, then inserts C before A. With index keys, the first position still has key zero but now represents C; input or component state can become associated with the wrong record. Stable record ids let React follow A as it moves. Index keys can be acceptable for a truly fixed list, but become risky when insertion, deletion or reordering is possible. > [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A cloakroom ticket > A ticket follows one person's coat even if staff rearrange the pegs. > > **How it maps:** A stable key identifies the same list item when its position among siblings changes; a peg position alone is like an array index. > > **Where it stops:** Keys only identify items within a particular sibling list. They do not globally locate components or preserve state after an item is removed. `key` is special React information, not a normal prop delivered to the child. If a `TaskRow` needs its record id, pass it separately, for example as an `id` prop as well as the key. Reusing the same data value for those two purposes is fine. ## Key takeaways - `filter` selects records; `map` transforms them into elements. - Put a stable key on the element returned directly by `map`. - Use data identity rather than changing positions or random values. - Pass an id separately if the child needs it; it cannot read `key` as an ordinary prop. ## Further reading - [Rendering lists — React](https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists) - [Array map — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/map)

lessons.title: Rendering should calculate, not change
lessons.summary: Separate rendering from committing and keep component calculations free of external changes.
lessons.body:
Writing JSX describes a desired result. It does not mean every function call immediately changes the page. Understanding React's **render** and **commit** stages makes it easier to avoid bugs caused by code that does work at the wrong time. ## Calculate first, update the DOM later A render is React calling components to calculate what their UI should look like. On an initial render React calls the root and the components it returns. On later updates, it calls components as needed to calculate a new result. A parent rendering can cause its children to render too. A commit is React applying the necessary changes to the browser's DOM. On an update, React compares the new description with the previous result; rendering does not mean replacing every DOM node. The browser then paints what is visible. Do not use the number of component function calls as a count of user actions or committed updates: React may repeat or discard render work. ## Keep render calculations pure A **pure render** returns the same UI for the same props, state and context inputs, without changing things that existed before it ran. State is a component's remembered data; the next lesson introduces it. Context is another React input mechanism covered later. A render calculation should read those inputs and return its description. Do not change received props, modify a module-level counter, send a request or write to the DOM during render. Those changes would be **side effects**, observable work beyond producing the returned value. Repeating a render could then repeat the work even without another interaction. Local mutation can be fine: a fresh array created during this render belongs only to this calculation. This component excerpt creates such an array, fills it and returns elements built from it. It leaves `tasks` and its records untouched. ```jsx function TaskNames({ tasks }) { const names = []; // Only this render owns this array. for (const task of tasks) { names.push(task.title.toUpperCase()); } return

{names.join(', ')}

; } ``` Given tasks titled `Read` and `Practise`, it displays `READ, PRACTISE`. Repeating the calculation with the same input gives the same result. The local `names` array starts fresh on every call; it does not accumulate titles across renders. By contrast, pushing into the `tasks` prop would modify data owned elsewhere. Sorting that same array in place would also modify it, even if the component only meant to change the display order. Later lessons show how to make copies for updates. > [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A draft shopping list > You can work out a shopping list on fresh paper without buying anything yet. > > **How it maps:** Rendering calculates a description; committing applies the agreed changes to the DOM. Work on a fresh local draft does not alter the shared starting information. > > **Where it stops:** React controls scheduling and may repeat calculations. A commit changes browser objects, not a real shopping basket, and is distinct from the browser painting pixels. ## Put actions at the right boundary An event handler is a natural place for work caused by a user action, such as submitting a request after a button press. Some synchronisation with outside systems belongs in an Effect, taught later. Moving every calculation into an Effect is not the goal: computing a title or filtered list from current inputs belongs in render. ## Key takeaways - Rendering calculates a description; committing updates the DOM. - A render can happen without a distinct committed change. - Treat props as immutable and avoid external changes during render. - Fresh local arrays can be built during a pure calculation. ## Further reading - [Render and commit — React](https://react.dev/learn/render-and-commit) - [Keeping components pure — React](https://react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure)

options.text: Both display 2 because they use the same function
options.explanation: Sharing a component definition does not automatically share its instance state.
Each component instance has its own state, so only the clicked instance changes.

options.text: Both stay 0 because the component reruns

Clicks are delivered to the activated instance; they are not distributed across identical components.

questions.prompt: A developer tries replacing useState with a local `let count = 0` inside Counter. Which statements explain why the local variable is insufficient and how useState helps? Select all that apply.

options.text: Changing count alone does not request a React render
options.explanation: A normal variable assignment is not a React state update.

options.text: The local variable persists automatically for the lifetime of the component instance
options.explanation: A local variable is initialised again when the component function runs.

options.text: The local value starts at zero again on another render
options.explanation: The declaration runs on each call; React does not retain ordinary local values as state.

options.text: The setter returned by useState both requests an update and lets React retain the new value
options.explanation: React state provides the memory and update scheduling that a local variable lacks.

questions.workedExample:
1. A function local belongs to that particular function call.
2. An assignment does not tell React to render again.
3. If another render occurs, the local declaration starts over.
4. useState supplies remembered instance data and a setter to request an update.
